item.title: Chesterton´s fence and being proud of what you have
item.description:
Chesterton’s fence is “the principle that reforms should not be made until the reasoning behind the existing state of affairs is understood.” Wikipedia. In software development think about is as don’t change code or an architecture before you understand why it is the way it is.

This is a good principle but I also started thinking about it from another perspective. When looking at an existing solution we as software engineers and developers can be very critical, this is not good, we have better ways to solve these kind of problems, let’s migrate, use a new technology. Yes we could probably improve the solution, the industry changes fast. But don’t forget to be proud! The solution is there, adds value, sometimes it has been doing that for a long time. Give it a chance and remember that when it was designed the decision were based on other requirements and possibilities than you have today. And this can help your reason. Do you really need to change it? Are the requirements that different now? Is this a dinosaur or could it be a technological shark that still is a good way to solve the problem?

item.title: Zeno´s migration
item.description: Migrations, changing technology like tools, libraries or bigger solutions, are sometimes straight forward, clearly define the starting and end point, plan and execute. But in more complex systems I see a tendency for migrations to fail when the plan is to “go from A to B” migration. System could be complex from a code or intergratin size perspective of view but even if it is a smaller technical migration complexity can be added also from organisational point of view, many people involved with different processes and different priorities.
